text: Seibei Iguchi's stipend has to cover two daughters and a mother whose mind is going, and it does not. He is a samurai of low rank at the turn of the nineteenth century, which here means an accountant of small humiliations: the work, the chores, the appearance a rank still obliges him to keep up. Yoji Yamada spends most of 129 minutes on that arithmetic. The sword is present and so is the code, but the pressure comes from Tomoe, a childhood friend returning to the household just as the feudal order that fixes Seibei's place in it begins to come apart. What binds him and what he wants are not the same thing, and neither can be set down cheaply. Japan's own academy gave its prize for a leading actor to the performance at the centre of it. Period drama, here, is a man counting money.

The family in Ilo Ilo pays a stranger to raise their son, and then has to watch her do it. Late 1990s Singapore: a busy working-class couple, one boy, and a woman hired from the Philippines to hold the household together while the parents are out earning. Anthony Chen keeps it to a hundred minutes and to four people in one apartment, shot as a place with not quite enough room for them. Nothing dramatic has to happen for the stakes to be plain. The boy's attachment is finite, the parents are elsewhere all day, and the employee is the one who is there. That is the whole of the risk, and it is enough. The film took Best Feature Film at the Golden Horse Awards and the Caméra d'Or, and Singapore sent it to the Academy Awards.

The father-in-law dies without warning, and grief turns out to arrive with a schedule, a house full of guests, and a set of procedures. Jūzō Itami gives the three days that follow 125 minutes and treats them as comedy, the kind that never once mocks the dead. Wabisuke and his wife are the ones in charge, which mostly means being watched. Everything a funeral requires has to be arranged in the correct order, and the inner lives of the people arranging it keep leaking out through the gaps in the procedure. Nobody stays sincere for long. Nobody stays insincere for long either. Set across three days in one house, it sits on Kinema Junpo's all-time list of Japanese films, though the reason to spend an evening with it is smaller and stranger: it is very funny about the moment a ritual stops carrying people and they have to carry it.

Genre listings call it a mystery, and the label holds only if a mystery is allowed to have no intention of resolving. Seijun Suzuki made it in 1980 and set it in an earlier Japan he feels no duty to keep tidy. A university professor and an unsettled friend with no fixed address circle one another for 144 minutes; romantic triangles form and loosen; the film advances by association rather than by plot. The length is the method. Strangeness given that much room stops announcing itself and becomes simply the weather of the film, which is why the mystery label is not wrong so much as beside the point. Kinema Junpo keeps it on its all-time list of Japanese films. Suzuki is not withholding an explanation; there was never going to be one.

A film star hands his pregnant mistress to a friend and asks him to marry her, and the friend agrees. Ginshiro is the star, and he is frightened: of his own reputation, and of Tachibana, the younger actor coming up behind him. Yasu is the friend. To keep the new household fed he goes into stunt work, which is where a film industry stores the labour it can afford to damage. Kinji Fukasaku made this in 1982 about the business he worked inside, and the tone swings hard, farce one minute and something colder the next, every cruelty routed through people being useful to one another. Nobody involved has illusions about the arrangement. That is what makes it funny, and what makes the laughter land badly. 108 minutes on a man's willingness to be spent, and the price at which he consents.

The apartment the two women are living in is not theirs; they are keeping it warm for a mother and daughter who are in hospital. Isa and Marie meet on the floor of a sweatshop, which is where Erick Zonca's film begins and what it never lets out of sight: piecework, hourly pay, the arithmetic of getting through a month. Then Marie takes up with Chriss, a nightclub owner whose money is the most persuasive thing about him, and Isa can see the shape of it from outside, which is a different thing from being able to say so. 113 minutes, nearly all of them given to the two of them. The European Film Awards went to it for the film and for a lead performance, and a César went to the cinematography, which is largely a matter of how it looks at small rooms and bad light.

Camille Claudel enters Auguste Rodin's studio as an apprentice, and the film gives itself 175 minutes to follow what that costs her. Bruno Nuytten directed it in 1988, and the length is not indulgence: apprenticeship first, then love, then the slow unfastening of a woman from the conditions that would let her keep working. Sculpture is the labour underneath all of it, a practice done with the hands, in materials that answer slowly, inside a world with settled opinions about which of the two of them was the artist. Most of the record the film carries is for performance, a Silver Bear for the lead and a César for an actor, and that is the right tell. It is built to be occupied rather than staged. Three hours inside one temperament, and it does not pretend the stay is comfortable.

Dora Carrington paints, Lytton Strachey writes, and the arrangement they make with each other has no available name. He wants men; she wants him; they set up house together regardless, and the household has to invent its terms as it goes, including terms for Ralph Partridge, the soldier Carrington intends to marry. Christopher Hampton directed it in 1995, in English, on a French production, and he films all of this as domestic business rather than scandal: rooms, work, the daily negotiation of who sleeps where and who is hurt by it. 121 minutes, mostly talk, and the talk is the pleasure. Articulate people failing to want the same thing turns out to be enough to hold a film. A Jury Prize and an acting award came of it. The interest is never whether the arrangement can work, only the labour of making it work.

Molly Roth is thirteen, and the politics of her country reach her the way weather does, through what the adults around her stop saying. Johannesburg in the 1960s, a white enclave, a house in which her parents' leftist commitments are the largest unspoken object. Her father disappears one night a step ahead of arrest. Her mother is detained not long after. Chris Menges films the rest from a girl's height: school friends who turn away, the family's Black friends becoming something else to her, the private cost of a public position she did not choose and cannot yet explain. Apartheid is the condition here, not the subject; the subject is what it does to the arrangements inside one family. 113 minutes, and it is a domestic drama in which nothing domestic holds. It took the Grand Prix at Cannes.

A film crew arrives in a village to make a picture about the Great Bengal Famine, and the village is not a set. The director inside Mrinal Sen's film is young and idealistic in the way that becomes a problem for everyone near him: he wants his picture to show that rural hardship did not end when the famine did, and he is right about that, which is exactly what makes his method hard to argue with and hard to defend. Shot in Bengali in 1979, 128 minutes. What is really under examination is the transaction, what a camera and a budget do to people who happen to live where a shoot has been scheduled, and what they are asked to give in the name of their own representation. It won a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize and India's National Film Award for best feature.

Three Australian lieutenants stand trial for shooting prisoners, under orders given by men who will not be in the courtroom. The war is the Boer War, the accused are colonial soldiers, and the General Staff needs the irregular conduct of the campaign to belong to somebody it can name. Most of Bruce Beresford's 107 minutes are procedure: testimony, objection, the slow assembly of a defence that fights considerably harder than anyone above it planned for. The force of the thing is entirely verbal, and the question at issue is less about three men than about how an empire distributes blame downward. Australia's own academy gave it awards for a leading performance, a supporting one, and the cinematography. Made in 1980, and the anger in it is administrative: precise, documented, filed.

There are no choirs here, no shafts of light, no miracle arranged for the camera. Alain Cavalier films the life of Thérèse of Lisieux in short vignettes on bare ground, in plain modern speech, at 94 minutes. She enters a Carmelite convent where her sisters are already nuns. Her idea, the little way to God, holds that holiness is available in the smallest acts a person has to hand, and Cavalier has built a form that matches it exactly: nothing accumulates, each scene completes itself and stops. What is left is faces, voices, cloth, and the sound of a rule being kept by people who chose it. The result sits closer to a list of days than to a story, which sounds austere and is in fact very close to tender. It holds a place on the César list for best film.

Two halves, two seasons, and no hinge offered between them: summer by the sea, winter in a village under snow. In the first, Nagisa and Natsuo meet at the water and manage only awkward words before wading into a rain-drenched ocean. In the second, Li, a screenwriter, reaches a snowbound village and stops at a guesthouse run by a man called Benzo. Sho Miyake gives both stories 89 minutes in total, so neither gets the room a conventional film would think sufficient, and that shortfall is the design. Whatever connects them has to be carried by weather, by pace, by the difference between rain on a beach and snow on a road. The whole film is a wager that a cut which explains nothing can still hold. Rhyme rather than plot. It carries a Golden Leopard.

The whole of this film is one downtown arcade in Buenos Aires: a lingerie shop, an importer's office, and the corridors between them. Ariel Makaroff, twenty-something, has walked away from architecture school and spends his days there, in his mother's shop and his brother's business, among people who have been trading in the same passage for years. Daniel Burman plays most of it as comedy, and the comedy is patient: nothing in the arcade is urgent, no one's plan is going anywhere, and the family's Jewish-Argentinean history is present the way foundations are present. Then the father who left when Ariel was an infant comes back to Argentina. 99 minutes, scaled deliberately small; no reckoning is announced, the shops just keep opening. It took a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize.
